name: Axial stress
description: Computes the normal (axial) stress in a member as force F divided by cross-sectional area A. It represents the internal force per unit area acting perpendicular to the section.
notes: With force in N and area in mm², the result comes out directly in MPa (N/mm²). Assumes the load is uniform over the section and passes through its centroid.

name: Normal strain
description: Gives the engineering normal strain as elongation ΔL divided by the original length L. It is a dimensionless measure of how much the material stretches relative to its initial size.
notes: Both lengths must share the same unit so the ratio is dimensionless. Valid for small strains; negative values indicate compression rather than stretching.

name: Young's modulus
description: Computes Young's modulus as stress divided by strain, the slope of the linear elastic part of the stress–strain curve. It quantifies a material's stiffness in tension or compression.
notes: Valid only in the linear elastic region below the proportional limit. Strain is dimensionless, so the modulus carries the same stress unit (MPa) as the input stress.

name: Shear stress
description: Gives the average shear stress as shear force V divided by the area A resisting shear. It measures the internal force per unit area acting parallel to the cross-section.
notes: Force in N and area in mm² give the result directly in MPa. This is an average value; actual shear stress is not uniform across the section.

name: Factor of safety
description: Computes the factor of safety as the ratio of ultimate (or yield) strength to the actual working stress. A value above 1 means the material is stronger than the applied load requires.
notes: Both stresses must use the same unit so the ratio is dimensionless. A value at or below 1 indicates failure; the reference strength should match the relevant failure mode.

name: Beam bending stress
description: The flexure formula gives the bending stress in a beam as M×c/I, where M is the bending moment, c the distance from the neutral axis, and I the moment of inertia. Stress is largest at the outer fibres.
notes: Keep units consistent (N·mm, mm, mm⁴) to get MPa. Valid for linear-elastic bending of straight beams with symmetric sections; stress varies linearly with distance from the neutral axis.

name: Moment of inertia (rectangle)
description: Gives the second moment of area of a rectangular section about its centroidal axis as b×h³/12, where b is the width and h the height parallel to bending. It measures resistance to bending.
notes: The cube on h means the dimension parallel to the bending direction dominates; swapping b and h changes the result. Axis is the centroidal axis, not an edge.

name: Moment of inertia (circle)
description: Computes the second moment of area of a solid circular section about a centroidal diameter as π×d⁴/64. It quantifies the section's resistance to bending and grows with the fourth power of diameter.
notes: For a solid circle only; a hollow shaft subtracts the inner diameter's contribution. This is the area moment about a diameter, not the polar moment about the centre.

name: Section modulus (rectangle)
description: Gives the elastic section modulus of a rectangle as b×h²/6, equal to its moment of inertia divided by the distance to the outer fibre. It links bending moment directly to maximum bending stress.
notes: The height h is squared, so the dimension parallel to bending governs. Divide the bending moment by this value to get the peak elastic bending stress.

name: Torsional shear stress
description: The torsion formula gives the shear stress in a shaft as T×r/J, where T is the torque, r the radial distance, and J the polar moment of inertia. Stress is maximum at the outer surface.
notes: Keep units consistent (N·mm, mm, mm⁴) for MPa. Valid for circular shafts in the elastic range; shear stress varies linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at r.

name: Polar moment of inertia (circle)
description: Computes the polar moment of inertia of a solid circular shaft as π×d⁴/32, describing its resistance to torsion. It is twice the diameter-axis area moment and grows with the fourth power of diameter.
notes: For a solid circle only; hollow shafts subtract the bore's contribution. Used with the torsion formula, not for bending, where the area moment about a diameter applies.

name: Hoop stress (thin cylinder)
description: Gives the circumferential (hoop) stress in a thin-walled pressure cylinder as p×r/t, from internal pressure p, inner radius r, and wall thickness t. It acts tangentially around the wall.
notes: Valid only for thin walls, roughly radius over thickness greater than 10. Hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress and usually governs the design.

name: Longitudinal stress (thin cylinder)
description: Gives the axial (longitudinal) stress in a thin-walled pressure cylinder as p×r/(2t), from internal pressure p, inner radius r, and wall thickness t. It acts along the cylinder's length.
notes: Valid only for thin walls (radius/thickness above about 10). This stress is half the hoop stress, so hoop stress usually controls sizing of the wall.

name: Helical spring rate
description: Computes the stiffness (spring rate) of a helical compression spring as G×d⁴/(8×n×Dm³), from shear modulus G, wire diameter d, active coils n, and mean coil diameter Dm. It is the force needed per unit deflection.
notes: Very sensitive to wire diameter (fourth power) and coil diameter (inverse cube). Keep G and diameters in consistent units; valid within the spring's elastic range.

name: Helical spring deflection
description: Gives the axial deflection of a helical compression spring under load F as 8×F×n×Dm³/(G×d⁴), from active coils n, mean coil diameter Dm, shear modulus G, and wire diameter d. It is the inverse of spring rate times force.
notes: Highly sensitive to coil and wire diameters; keep units consistent. Valid in the elastic range only, before the coils bottom out or yield.

name: Power from torque and speed
description: Computes mechanical shaft power in kW from torque in N·m and rotational speed in rpm using T×rpm/9549. The constant 9549 combines the 2π/60 conversion from rpm to rad/s and the watt-to-kilowatt factor.
notes: Requires torque in N·m and speed in rpm exactly; the result is kW. The 9549 constant already bakes in the unit conversions, so do not convert rpm separately.

name: Torque from power and speed
description: Gives shaft torque in N·m from power in kW and speed in rpm using 9549×P/rpm, the inverse of the power-from-torque relation. For a fixed power, torque falls as rotational speed rises.
notes: Power must be in kW and speed in rpm; the result is N·m. The 9549 constant embeds the rpm-to-rad/s and kW-to-W conversions, so use those units directly.

name: Gear ratio
description: Computes the gear ratio as the number of teeth on the driven gear divided by the teeth on the driving gear. A ratio above 1 means speed is reduced and torque is multiplied.
notes: Tooth counts are integers, giving a dimensionless ratio. Output speed is input speed divided by this ratio; ideal torque is multiplied by it, ignoring friction losses.

name: Belt length (open drive)
description: Estimates the length of a belt on an open (non-crossed) two-pulley drive as 2C + π(D1+D2)/2 + (D2−D1)²/(4C), from centre distance C and the two pulley diameters. It accounts for the wrap around each pulley.
notes: This is an approximation for an open belt; crossed belts use a different formula. All lengths must share the same unit; accuracy drops when the pulleys differ greatly in size.

name: Bolt tightening torque
description: Estimates the tightening torque for a bolt as K×d×F, from the torque coefficient K, nominal diameter d, and target preload F. It relates the wrench torque to the clamping force produced.
notes: K (typically around 0.2) lumps together thread and head friction and varies with lubrication and finish. Result is in N·mm here; only a fraction of the torque becomes preload.

name: Pressure vessel wall thickness
description: Gives the minimum wall thickness of a thin cylindrical pressure vessel as p×D/(2S), from internal pressure p, inner diameter D, and allowable stress S. It is set by keeping hoop stress within the allowable limit.
notes: A thin-wall estimate with no corrosion or weld-joint allowance; real designs add those margins. Keep pressure and allowable stress in the same unit (MPa) so thickness matches D's unit.

name: Fillet weld throat thickness
description: Gives the effective throat thickness of an equal-leg fillet weld as 0.707 times the leg length. The factor is sin 45°, the shortest distance from the weld root to the face, which carries the stress.
notes: Applies to equal-leg (45°) fillet welds; unequal legs need the actual throat geometry. Weld strength calculations use this throat, not the larger leg dimension.

name: Spring-mass natural frequency
description: Computes the undamped natural frequency of a spring-mass system in hertz as (1/2π)×sqrt(k/m), from spring constant k and mass m. Stiffer springs raise the frequency and heavier masses lower it.
notes: Gives frequency in Hz; multiply by 2π for angular frequency in rad/s. This is the undamped value, so damping slightly reduces the actual oscillation frequency.

name: Damping ratio
description: Gives the damping ratio of a spring-mass-damper system as c/(2×sqrt(k×m)), comparing the damping coefficient to critical damping. It classifies the response as under-, critically, or over-damped.
notes: Dimensionless: below 1 is under-damped (oscillatory), equal to 1 is critical, above 1 is over-damped. Keep c, k, and m in consistent SI units.

name: Pipe flow velocity
description: Computes the mean flow velocity in a pipe as volumetric flow rate Q divided by the cross-sectional area A. It is the average speed across the section from continuity.
notes: Keep flow rate and area in consistent units (m³/s and m²) for m/s. This is the bulk average; the true profile peaks at the centre and is zero at the wall.

name: Mechanical power
description: Gives the mechanical power as force F times velocity v, the rate at which the force does work. When force and motion are aligned, this is the instantaneous power delivered.
notes: Force in N and velocity in m/s give power in watts. Assumes force and velocity are parallel; otherwise use only the force component along the direction of motion.

name: Angle of twist
description: Gives the angular twist of a circular shaft under torque as T×L/(J×G), from torque T, length L, polar moment of inertia J, and shear modulus G. Longer or softer shafts twist more.
notes: Result is in radians; multiply by 180/π for degrees. Valid for a uniform circular shaft in the elastic range with constant torque along its length.

name: Thermal expansion of length
description: Computes the change in length of a solid from heating as L×α×ΔT, from original length L, linear expansion coefficient α, and temperature change ΔT. The bar lengthens on heating and shortens on cooling.
notes: This is linear (1-D) expansion; area and volume expand at roughly 2α and 3α. Keep α consistent with ΔT (per kelvin); the change shares L's length unit.

name: Section modulus (circle)
description: Gives the elastic section modulus of a solid circular section as π×d³/32, equal to its area moment of inertia divided by the outer radius. Dividing bending moment by it yields the peak bending stress.
notes: For a solid circle in bending; hollow sections need the bored form. Note this uses d³/32 for bending, distinct from the polar-related d³ modulus used in torsion.

name: Max bending moment (center load)
description: Gives the maximum bending moment of a simply supported beam with a central point load as F×L/4, occurring under the load at mid-span. Larger loads or longer spans increase the peak moment.
notes: Applies to a simply supported beam with a single central load only; other load positions or supports change the formula. L is the full span between supports.

name: Von Mises stress (plane stress)
description: Computes the equivalent von Mises stress for plane stress as sqrt(σx² − σx·σy + σy² + 3τxy²), combining the two normal stresses and the shear stress into a single value for comparison with yield strength.
notes: Valid for the plane-stress (2-D) case only; three-dimensional states need the full expression. Yielding is predicted when this equivalent stress reaches the material's yield strength.

name: Column slenderness ratio
description: Gives a column's slenderness ratio as effective length L divided by the radius of gyration sqrt(I/A), from moment of inertia I and cross-sectional area A. Higher values mean a more buckling-prone column.
notes: Dimensionless; keep I and A in consistent units. Use the effective length that reflects the end conditions, and the least radius of gyration governs buckling.

name: Ball bearing dynamic life
description: Gives the basic rating life of a ball bearing in millions of revolutions as (C/P)³, from the dynamic load rating C and equivalent load P. Reducing the load sharply extends bearing life.
notes: Uses the exponent 3 for ball bearings; roller bearings use 10/3. Result is in millions of revolutions (L10, 90% reliability); C and P must share the same force unit.

name: Helical spring shear stress
description: Gives the nominal torsional shear stress in helical spring wire as 8×F×Dm/(π×d³), from axial load F, mean coil diameter Dm, and wire diameter d. Thinner wire or larger coils raise the stress.
notes: This is the basic stress without the Wahl curvature correction, which increases the true peak. Keep loads and diameters consistent so the result comes out in MPa.

name: Hydraulic cylinder force
description: Computes the output force of a hydraulic cylinder as pressure p times the piston area π×d²/4, from the supply pressure and piston diameter. Larger bore or higher pressure gives more force.
notes: This is the extend force on the full piston face; the rod side has less area and lower force. With pressure in MPa and diameter in mm the result is in newtons.

name: Critical damping coefficient
description: Gives the critical damping coefficient of a spring-mass system as 2×sqrt(k×m), the damping value that just prevents oscillation. Dividing the actual damping by it yields the damping ratio.
notes: At this value the system returns to rest fastest without overshooting. Keep k and m in consistent SI units; the result carries units of N·s/m.
